justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 261.5 was anchored closely to the last observed price, with only a very small drift applied since overnight or intraday moves in liquid markets tend to mean-revert around recent levels. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 262.5, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with a modest bullish bias but without strong directional conviction. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 264.0 extends that gentle upward trend further, consistent with a rough approximation of long-run expected returns on equity-linked or broadly diversified instruments, assuming no major regime change.

The width of the confidence intervals was primarily driven by realized volatility assumptions scaled to each time horizon. For the one-day interval, I used a relatively tight band of roughly plus or minus 6–7 points, consistent with typical daily price swings under normal market conditions. For the one-week horizon, I widened the interval to approximately plus or minus 12–13 points, scaling uncertainty by roughly the square root of time, as is standard in financial modeling. The one-month interval, at plus or minus 24 points, reflects the continued application of this scaling principle. I also incorporated some additional uncertainty at longer horizons to account for the possibility of macro regime shifts or structural breaks that don't show up cleanly in short-run volatility estimates.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift toward aggressive tightening, geopolitical escalation, or a liquidity event in credit markets could all produce moves well beyond the lower bounds. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season, a dovish pivot from major central banks, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical risk premium could produce outsized gains. Fat-tailed events — the kind that occur far more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest — are the primary reason these stated intervals should be treated as indicative rather than exhaustive. In practice, roughly 10–15% of monthly outcomes in equity-related instruments historically fall outside what naive volatility scaling would predict.
